learningObjectives.title: 9.3 Gibbs Free Energy and Thermodynamic Favorability

questions.q: A 1.0 mol sample of H₂O undergoes each of the following changes at a constant pressure of 1.0 atm. Which change gives the greatest increase in the entropy of the H₂O?
options: Liquid water warming from 0°C to 100°C
Ice melting to form liquid water at 0°C
Steam condensing to form liquid water at 100°C
Liquid water vaporizing to steam at 100°C
optionWhy: A student who thinks entropy changes only when the temperature changes picks this, as the only change listed with a temperature rise. Warming the liquid does increase its entropy, but far less than vaporization, in which the molecules become dispersed through a volume more than a thousand times larger.

A student who equates entropy with visible disorder picks this, because the ordered arrangement of the solid is lost. The molecules of the liquid remain close together, so the entropy increase on melting, about 22 J/(mol·K), is much smaller than that on vaporization, about 109 J/(mol·K).

A student who thinks a process that releases energy increases the entropy of the substance picks this. Condensation releases energy to the surroundings, but the H₂O molecules become far less dispersed, so the entropy of the H₂O decreases.

Vaporization disperses the molecules from a liquid into a gas that occupies a far larger volume, so it produces the greatest dispersal of matter: about 109 J/(mol·K) for H₂O, compared with about 22 J/(mol·K) for melting and about 23 J/(mol·K) for warming the liquid from 0°C to 100°C. Condensation decreases the entropy of the H₂O.
questions.explain: Vaporization disperses the molecules from a liquid into a gas that occupies a far larger volume, so it produces the greatest dispersal of matter: about 109 J/(mol·K) for H₂O, compared with about 22 J/(mol·K) for melting and about 23 J/(mol·K) for warming the liquid from 0°C to 100°C. Condensation decreases the entropy of the H₂O.

questions.q: The diagram represents a sample of helium gas in two connected rigid bulbs before and after the valve between the bulbs is opened. The temperature of the helium is the same before and after. Which claim about the entropy of the helium is supported by the diagram?
options: It decreases, because the atoms are less crowded and collide less often
It stays the same, because the average kinetic energy is unchanged
It stays the same, because the number of gas atoms is unchanged
It increases, because the same atoms move within twice the volume
optionWhy: A student who equates entropy with how chaotic and crowded a system looks picks this. The atoms are less crowded after the valve is opened, but being able to move within a larger space makes the matter more dispersed, so the entropy increases.

A student who thinks entropy changes only when the temperature changes picks this. The average kinetic energy of the atoms is unchanged at constant temperature, but the atoms occupy twice the volume, and this dispersal of matter increases the entropy.

A student who applies the moles-of-gas rule for reactions to every process picks this. Eight atoms are present before and after, but that rule is for reactions; a fixed amount of gas gains entropy when its volume increases at constant temperature.

The diagram shows the same eight atoms, first confined to one bulb and then spread through two bulbs of equal size. At constant temperature, a gas whose particles are able to move within a larger space has its matter more dispersed, so the entropy of the helium increases.
questions.explain: The diagram shows the same eight atoms, first confined to one bulb and then spread through two bulbs of equal size. At constant temperature, a gas whose particles are able to move within a larger space has its matter more dispersed, so the entropy of the helium increases.

questions.q: The table gives thermodynamic data at 298 K for the species in the reaction 2 C(s, graphite) + O₂(g) → 2 CO(g). Based on the data in the table, what is ΔS° for the reaction?
options: +395.4 J/(mol_rxn·K)
−221.0 J/(mol_rxn·K)
+178.8 J/(mol_rxn·K)
−178.8 J/(mol_rxn·K)
optionWhy: A student who takes the entropy of an element in its standard state to be zero, as its ΔH°_f is, picks this: 2(197.7) − 0. S° values are absolute entropies, so 2(5.7) + 205.2 = 216.6 J/K for the graphite and O₂ must be subtracted.

A student who thinks the entropy change is found from the enthalpy-of-formation data picks this: 2(−110.5) − 0 = −221.0. That number is ΔH° for the reaction in kJ/mol_rxn; ΔS° comes from the S° column.

ΔS° is calculated from the S° column alone: 2(197.7) − [2(5.7) + 205.2] = 395.4 − 216.6 = +178.8 J/(mol_rxn·K). The elements have ΔH°_f = 0 but nonzero absolute entropies, and each S° is multiplied by its coefficient.

A student who subtracts the products' entropies from the reactants' entropies picks this: 216.6 − 395.4. ΔS° is the entropy after the process minus the entropy before it, 395.4 − 216.6 = +178.8 J/(mol_rxn·K).
questions.explain: ΔS° is calculated from the S° column alone: 2(197.7) − [2(5.7) + 205.2] = 395.4 − 216.6 = +178.8 J/(mol_rxn·K). The elements have ΔH°_f = 0 but nonzero absolute entropies, and each S° is multiplied by its coefficient.
questions.working: Only the S° column is used. ΔS° = ΣS°_products − ΣS°_reactants = 2 S°(CO) − [2 S°(C, graphite) + S°(O₂)] = 2(197.7) − [2(5.7) + 205.2] = 395.4 − 216.6 = +178.8 J/(mol_rxn·K). The positive sign fits the particulate picture: 1 mol of gas and a solid form 2 mol of gas.

questions.q: For the reaction 2 SO₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2 SO₃(g), ΔS° = −188.0 J/(mol_rxn·K) at 298 K. The table gives the standard molar entropies of SO₂(g) and O₂(g) at 298 K. What is the standard molar entropy of SO₃(g)?
optionWhy: A student who uses each S° value once, ignoring the coefficients, picks this: −188.0 + 248.2 + 205.2. Both SO₂ and SO₃ have coefficient 2, so S°(SO₂) is doubled and the result is divided by 2.
A student who takes S° of the element O₂(g) to be zero picks this, solving 2 S°(SO₃) = −188.0 + 2(248.2). O₂(g) has S° = 205.2 J/(mol·K), which must be included with the reactants.
A student who writes ΔS° as reactants minus products picks this, solving −188.0 = 701.6 − 2 S°(SO₃). ΔS° is products minus reactants, which gives 256.8 J/(mol·K).

questions.q: For a hypothetical reaction, ΔH° = +40.0 kJ/mol_rxn and ΔS° = −50.0 J/(mol_rxn·K) at 298 K, and these values change little with temperature. A student predicts that heating the reaction mixture to 1000 K will make the reaction thermodynamically favored. Which evaluation of the prediction is correct?
options: It is right: at a high temperature the TΔS° term dominates, so ΔG° becomes negative
It is right: heating makes the reaction go faster, so it becomes more favored
It is wrong: ΔG° stays positive at every temperature, as ΔH° > 0 and ΔS° < 0
It is wrong: with ΔS° < 0 the reaction is favored only at low temperatures, so cool it
optionWhy: A student who thinks heating always makes a process more favored picks this. TΔS° does grow with T, but ΔS° is negative, so −TΔS° adds a positive amount: ΔG° = +90.0 kJ/mol_rxn at 1000 K.
A student who equates a fast reaction with a favored one picks this. Heating does increase the rate, but favorability depends on ΔG°, which is positive at every temperature here.
Both terms of ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° are positive: ΔH° = +40.0 kJ/mol_rxn and −TΔS° = +T(0.0500 kJ/(mol_rxn·K)). At 1000 K, ΔG° = +90.0 kJ/mol_rxn; heating only makes ΔG° more positive.
A student who remembers 'negative ΔS°, favored at low T' without the condition ΔH° < 0 picks this. Here ΔH° > 0, so ΔG° = 40.0 + T(0.0500) is positive at low temperatures as well.
questions.explain: Both terms of ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° are positive: ΔH° = +40.0 kJ/mol_rxn and −TΔS° = +T(0.0500 kJ/(mol_rxn·K)). At 1000 K, ΔG° = +90.0 kJ/mol_rxn; heating only makes ΔG° more positive.
questions.working: ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° = 40.0 + T(0.0500). Both terms are positive at every T: at 298 K, +54.9; at 1000 K, +90.0 kJ/mol_rxn. ΔH° > 0 and ΔS° < 0: unfavored at all temperatures.

questions.q: The table gives ΔH° and ΔS° at 298 K for four processes. Which process has the most negative ΔG° at 298 K?
options: Process W
Process X
Process Y
Process Z
optionWhy: A student who judges favorability by ΔH° alone picks this, because Process W has the most negative ΔH°, −45.0 kJ/mol_rxn. Its ΔS° is −100.0 J/(mol_rxn·K), so −TΔS° = +29.8 kJ/mol_rxn and ΔG° is only −15.2 kJ/mol_rxn.

ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°, with ΔS° converted to kJ. Process X: −35.0 − 298(0.0400) = −46.9 kJ/mol_rxn. The others: W −15.2, Y −38.8, Z +9.7. Process X has the most negative ΔG°: it is exothermic and its entropy increases, so both terms favor it.

A student who judges favorability by ΔS° alone picks this, because Process Y has the largest ΔS°, +80.0 J/(mol_rxn·K). Its ΔH° is only −15.0 kJ/mol_rxn, so ΔG° = −15.0 − 23.8 = −38.8 kJ/mol_rxn, less negative than for Process X.

A student who treats a negative ΔS° as favorable, like a negative ΔH°, picks this, calculating ΔH° + TΔS° = −35.0 − 44.7 = −79.7 kJ/mol_rxn. With the correct sign, ΔG° = −35.0 + 44.7 = +9.7 kJ/mol_rxn: Process Z is not even favored.
questions.explain: ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°, with ΔS° converted to kJ. Process X: −35.0 − 298(0.0400) = −46.9 kJ/mol_rxn. The others: W −15.2, Y −38.8, Z +9.7. Process X has the most negative ΔG°: it is exothermic and its entropy increases, so both terms favor it.

questions.q: At 25°C and 1 atm, the conversion C(diamond) → C(graphite) has ΔG° = −2.9 kJ/mol_rxn, yet diamonds show no measurable conversion to graphite. A student explains this observation by proposing that diamond and graphite are at equilibrium. Which evaluation of the student's explanation is correct?
options: Correct: no net change is observed, so the forward and reverse conversions must have equal rates
Incorrect: ΔG° is so close to zero that the conversion has too little driving force to be fast
Correct: the carbon atoms have stopped reacting, which is what being at equilibrium means
Incorrect: the conversion is favored, but its activation energy is so high that no change is detected
optionWhy: A student who takes the absence of observable change as proof of equilibrium picks this. No change is observed because the favored conversion is immeasurably slow, not because two opposing processes are occurring at equal rates.

A student who thinks the size of ΔG° sets the rate picks this. The rate of a process depends on its activation energy, not on the magnitude of ΔG°; reactions with ΔG° values close to zero can be fast, and reactions with very negative ΔG° values can be immeasurably slow.

A student who thinks equilibrium means that reaction has stopped picks this. At equilibrium the forward and reverse processes continue at equal rates. Diamond is not converting at a detectable rate because of a high activation energy, although the conversion is favored.

ΔG° < 0, so the conversion to graphite is thermodynamically favored, and a system at equilibrium would not consist of unconverted diamond. The absence of change is explained by a very high activation energy for rearranging the bonded carbon atoms: the process is under kinetic control. A process that does not proceed at a noticeable rate is not thereby at equilibrium.
questions.explain: ΔG° < 0, so the conversion to graphite is thermodynamically favored, and a system at equilibrium would not consist of unconverted diamond. The absence of change is explained by a very high activation energy for rearranging the bonded carbon atoms: the process is under kinetic control. A process that does not proceed at a noticeable rate is not thereby at equilibrium.

questions.q: The diagram represents a mixture of X₂(g) and Y₂(g) kept in a sealed container at 298 K, when the mixture is prepared and one year later. When a spark is passed through an identical mixture, the gases react rapidly and almost completely to form XY(g). Which statement correctly describes what the diagram shows about the mixture kept at 298 K?
options: The composition is the same at both times, so the mixture has reached equilibrium
Only X₂ and Y₂ are present at both times, so no measurable reaction has occurred
No XY is present at either time, so the formation of XY is not favored at 298 K
The molecules are unchanged at both times, so X₂ and Y₂ molecules are not colliding
optionWhy: A student who takes a constant composition as proof of equilibrium picks this. An equilibrium mixture for this reaction would consist almost entirely of XY, as the sparked mixture shows. A mixture of unreacted X₂ and Y₂ is not at equilibrium; it is reacting too slowly to detect.

Both boxes contain four X₂ and four Y₂ molecules and no XY, so no measurable amount of product has formed in a year. Because the same mixture reacts almost completely once a spark starts it, the formation of XY is favored; the unreacted mixture is an example of a favored process that does not occur at a measurable rate.

A student who thinks a favored reaction must be seen to happen picks this. The absence of XY shows only that the reaction is extremely slow at 298 K. A spark supplies activation energy, not favorability, and once started the reaction goes almost to completion.

A student who thinks every collision leads to reaction picks this. Gas molecules collide constantly; the molecules are unchanged because almost none of the collisions has enough energy to overcome the activation energy.
questions.explain: Both boxes contain four X₂ and four Y₂ molecules and no XY, so no measurable amount of product has formed in a year. Because the same mixture reacts almost completely once a spark starts it, the formation of XY is favored; the unreacted mixture is an example of a favored process that does not occur at a measurable rate.

questions.q: At 450 K, ΔG° = −20.0 kJ/mol_rxn for reaction 1. At the same temperature, the equilibrium constant of reaction 2 is exactly 10 times the equilibrium constant of reaction 1. What is ΔG° for reaction 2 at 450 K?
options: −25.7 kJ/mol_rxn
−23.7 kJ/mol_rxn
−11.4 kJ/mol_rxn
−28.6 kJ/mol_rxn
optionWhy: A student who uses T = 298 K because of the ° symbol picks this: RT ln 10 = (8.314)(298)(2.303) J/mol = 5.7 kJ/mol. The temperature in the equation is the temperature of the system, 450 K, which gives a change of 8.6 kJ/mol.
A student who treats ln as log picks this: log 10 = 1, so the change is taken as RT = (8.314)(450) J/mol = 3.7 kJ/mol. The equation uses the natural logarithm, and ln 10 = 2.303.
A student who thinks ΔG° and K rise and fall together picks this, adding RT ln 10 = 8.6 kJ/mol for the larger K. The negative sign in ΔG° = −RT ln K means a larger K gives a more negative ΔG°.
Because ΔG° = −RT ln K, multiplying K by 10 changes ΔG° by −RT ln 10 = −(8.314)(450)(2.303) J/mol = −8.6 kJ/mol, so ΔG° for reaction 2 is −20.0 − 8.6 = −28.6 kJ/mol_rxn.
questions.explain: Because ΔG° = −RT ln K, multiplying K by 10 changes ΔG° by −RT ln 10 = −(8.314)(450)(2.303) J/mol = −8.6 kJ/mol, so ΔG° for reaction 2 is −20.0 − 8.6 = −28.6 kJ/mol_rxn.
questions.working: ΔG°₂ = −RT ln K₂ = −RT ln(10 K₁) = −RT ln K₁ − RT ln 10 = ΔG°₁ − RT ln 10. RT ln 10 = (8.314 J/(mol·K))(450 K)(2.303) = 8.61 × 10³ J/mol = 8.6 kJ/mol. ΔG°₂ = −20.0 − 8.6 = −28.6 kJ/mol_rxn. A larger K goes with a more negative ΔG°.

questions.q: For a gas-phase reaction in which one reactant molecule forms one product molecule, ΔG° = −1.0 kJ/mol_rxn at 298 K. At 298 K, RT = 2.5 kJ/mol. A student claims that at equilibrium at 298 K nearly all of the reactant will have been converted to product. Which evaluation of the claim is correct?
options: The claim is not supported: ΔG° is close to zero, so K is close to 1
The claim is supported: ΔG° is negative, so the reaction goes to completion
The claim is not supported: ΔG° is negative, so K is less than 1
The claim is not supported: ΔG° is not zero, so equilibrium is not reached
optionWhy: −ΔG°/RT = 1.0/2.5 = 0.40, so K = e^(0.40) ≈ 1.5. ΔG° is close to zero (its magnitude is smaller than RT), so K is close to 1, and the equilibrium mixture contains comparable amounts of reactant and product (about 60% product), not nearly all product.

A student who thinks any reaction with ΔG° < 0 goes essentially to completion picks this. The sign shows only that K > 1; the size of ΔG° compared with RT shows that K ≈ 1.5, so much of the reactant remains.

A student who matches a negative ΔG° with a K less than 1 picks this. ΔG° < 0 gives K > 1 (here about 1.5); the claim fails because K is only slightly greater than 1, not because the reactant is favored.
A student who thinks ΔG° must be zero at equilibrium picks this. The system does reach equilibrium, with K = e^(0.40) ≈ 1.5; ΔG° determines the value of K, not whether equilibrium can be reached.
questions.explain: −ΔG°/RT = 1.0/2.5 = 0.40, so K = e^(0.40) ≈ 1.5. ΔG° is close to zero (its magnitude is smaller than RT), so K is close to 1, and the equilibrium mixture contains comparable amounts of reactant and product (about 60% product), not nearly all product.

questions.q: Solid MX contains M⁺ and X⁻ ions. Solid QZ contains Q²⁺ and Z²⁻ ions that are about the same sizes as M⁺ and X⁻. A student predicts that QZ is more soluble in water than MX because, according to Coulomb's law, the ions of QZ attract water molecules more strongly. Which evaluation of the student's prediction is correct?
options: Unreliable: the ions in solid QZ also attract one another more strongly, so the overall effect is uncertain
Reliable: stronger attractions to water release more energy, and a more exothermic dissolution is more favored
Unreliable: water molecules are neutral, so the charge of an ion has no effect on its attraction to water
Unreliable: the ions in solid QZ attract one another more strongly, so QZ must be the less soluble solid
optionWhy: The more highly charged ions do interact more strongly with water, which favors dissolving, but by the same law they attract one another more strongly in the solid, which opposes it, and they also restrict the surrounding water molecules more. These contributions to ΔG° of dissolution have opposite signs and largely cancel, so the solubility cannot be predicted from one factor.

A student who thinks favorability is decided by the energy released picks this. The energy released by ion-water attractions is offset by the larger energy needed to separate the Q²⁺ and Z²⁻ ions, and the entropy contributions matter too, so the total ΔG° cannot be predicted this way.

A student who treats water as a passive medium picks this. Water molecules are polar, and the ion-dipole attraction is stronger for more highly charged ions. The prediction is unreliable for a different reason: the attractions within the solid are stronger as well.

A student who thinks the attractions within the solid alone decide solubility picks this. The stronger attractions in solid QZ are opposed by stronger ion-water attractions, and these contributions largely cancel, so it is not possible to conclude that QZ is less soluble.
questions.explain: The more highly charged ions do interact more strongly with water, which favors dissolving, but by the same law they attract one another more strongly in the solid, which opposes it, and they also restrict the surrounding water molecules more. These contributions to ΔG° of dissolution have opposite signs and largely cancel, so the solubility cannot be predicted from one factor.

questions.q: The diagram shows a student's particle model of the dissolution of MgCl₂(s) in water. From the model, the student predicts that ΔS° for the dissolution is positive, but the measured ΔS° is negative. Which feature of the dissolution, missing from the student's model, best accounts for the negative ΔS°?
options: The release of energy to the surroundings, which lowers the entropy of the solution
The joining of Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻ ions into MgCl₂ molecules, which lowers the particle count
The disappearance of the ions as they dissolve, which leaves less matter to disperse
The ordered arrangement of water molecules around each ion, which restricts their motion
optionWhy: A student who thinks the entropy change follows the direction of energy transfer picks this. The dissolution of MgCl₂ does release energy, but the sign of ΔS° is decided by the dispersal of the ions and the restriction of the water molecules, not by the sign of ΔH°.

A student who thinks a dissolved ionic compound exists as intact units picks this. MgCl₂ is present in solution as separate Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻ ions, as the model shows; the feature that the model omits is the water.

A student who thinks dissolved particles are no longer there picks this. All the ions remain in the solution, dispersed among the water molecules; the entropy decrease comes from the water molecules that are held around the ions.

The model draws only the ions, which become more dispersed, and leaves out the solvent. Water molecules are strongly attracted to the small, highly charged Mg²⁺ ion and to the Cl⁻ ions and are held in oriented positions around them, so the water becomes less free to move. For MgCl₂ this negative contribution to ΔS° outweighs the positive contribution from dispersing the ions.
questions.explain: The model draws only the ions, which become more dispersed, and leaves out the solvent. Water molecules are strongly attracted to the small, highly charged Mg²⁺ ion and to the Cl⁻ ions and are held in oriented positions around them, so the water becomes less free to move. For MgCl₂ this negative contribution to ΔS° outweighs the positive contribution from dispersing the ions.

questions.q: The diagram shows standard free energies for a coupled system in which the conversion of WP to W and P drives the formation of XY through the intermediate XP. For the reaction WP → W + P, ΔG° = −38 kJ/mol_rxn. Based on the diagram, what is ΔG° for the reaction X + Y → XY?
options: −20 kJ/mol_rxn
−58 kJ/mol_rxn
+38 kJ/mol_rxn
+18 kJ/mol_rxn
optionWhy: A student who thinks coupling gives the formation of XY itself the coupled system's negative ΔG° picks this. −20 kJ/mol_rxn is ΔG° for the overall reaction, which includes WP → W + P; X + Y → XY on its own is unfavorable.

A student who removes WP → W + P from the overall reaction without changing the sign of its ΔG° picks this: −20 + (−38) = −58 kJ/mol_rxn. Removing a reaction means adding its reverse, ΔG° = +38 kJ/mol_rxn.

A student who thinks the favorable reaction hands over exactly the free energy the unfavorable reaction needs picks this. The overall ΔG° is −20 kJ/mol_rxn, not zero, so ΔG° for forming XY is +18 kJ/mol_rxn, smaller in magnitude than the −38 kJ/mol_rxn of WP → W + P.

The diagram gives ΔG° = −20 kJ/mol_rxn for the overall reaction X + Y + WP → XY + W + P. Subtracting WP → W + P (adding its reverse, +38 kJ/mol_rxn) leaves X + Y → XY with ΔG° = −20 + 38 = +18 kJ/mol_rxn, an unfavorable reaction.
questions.explain: The diagram gives ΔG° = −20 kJ/mol_rxn for the overall reaction X + Y + WP → XY + W + P. Subtracting WP → W + P (adding its reverse, +38 kJ/mol_rxn) leaves X + Y → XY with ΔG° = −20 + 38 = +18 kJ/mol_rxn, an unfavorable reaction.
questions.working: From the diagram, the overall coupled reaction X + Y + WP → XY + W + P has ΔG° = −20 − 0 = −20 kJ/mol_rxn. X + Y → XY = (overall) + (reverse of WP → W + P): ΔG° = −20 kJ/mol_rxn + (+38 kJ/mol_rxn) = +18 kJ/mol_rxn.

questions.q: A biology text states: "ATP stores energy in a high-energy phosphate bond, and this energy is released when the bond is broken, driving reactions coupled to the conversion of ATP to ADP." Which statement best evaluates how well this description represents the particulate-level origin of the energy released?
options: It is accurate, because energy is stored in the P–O bond and is released when that bond is broken
It is accurate, because the P–O bond in ATP is unusually strong and so releases more energy as it breaks
It is misleading, because breaking a bond absorbs energy; the release comes from new bonds and interactions forming
It is misleading, because breaking a bond absorbs energy, so converting ATP to ADP is unfavorable overall
optionWhy: A student who thinks energy is stored in bonds and released when they break picks this. Bond breaking is endothermic; energy is released only as bonds and attractions form.
A student who reads 'high-energy bond' as 'strong bond' picks this. A stronger bond needs more energy to break, not less; the term refers to the overall reaction's large negative ΔG°.

Breaking any bond, including the P–O bond in ATP, requires energy. The conversion of ATP to ADP is favorable overall because the bonds and interactions formed in the products are stronger overall than those broken, so the description misplaces the source of the energy.

A student who applies 'bond breaking absorbs energy' to the whole reaction picks this. The conversion of ATP to ADP is favorable overall, which is why it can be coupled to unfavorable reactions; the products' new bonds and interactions must be counted.
questions.explain: Breaking any bond, including the P–O bond in ATP, requires energy. The conversion of ATP to ADP is favorable overall because the bonds and interactions formed in the products are stronger overall than those broken, so the description misplaces the source of the energy.

questions.q: A cell contains a Cu electrode in Cu(NO₃)₂(aq) and a Ni electrode in Ni(NO₃)₂(aq), joined by a salt bridge and by wires. While the cell operates, the reaction Cu(s) + Ni²⁺(aq) → Cu²⁺(aq) + Ni(s) occurs; this reaction is thermodynamically unfavored. Which classification of the cell, with its justification, is correct?
options: Galvanic, because it has two different metal electrodes joined by a salt bridge
Galvanic, because electrons flow through the wires from one electrode to the other
Electrolytic, because both of its half-cells contain solutions of dissolved electrolytes
Electrolytic, because the unfavored reaction is driven by an outside power supply
optionWhy: A student who classifies a cell by its components picks this. The same two half-cells can form a galvanic or an electrolytic cell; what decides is whether the reaction that occurs is favored or unfavored.
A student who thinks electron flow shows that a cell is galvanic picks this. Electrons flow through the external circuit in electrolytic cells too, pushed by the power supply.

A student who takes 'electrolytic' to mean 'containing electrolytes' picks this. The classification is right but the reason is not: galvanic cells contain electrolyte solutions too. The cell is electrolytic because its reaction is unfavored and must be driven.

Galvanic cells use thermodynamically favored reactions; electrolytic cells use unfavored reactions driven by external electrical energy. Since the unfavored reaction occurs, the wires must connect the cell to a power supply.
questions.explain: Galvanic cells use thermodynamically favored reactions; electrolytic cells use unfavored reactions driven by external electrical energy. Since the unfavored reaction occurs, the wires must connect the cell to a power supply.

questions.q: The reaction Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s) is thermodynamically favored. In the cell shown, a power supply drives electrons through the external circuit in the directions of the arrows. Which statement describes what happens at the Zn electrode while the power supply operates?
options: Zn²⁺ ions are reduced, so zinc metal builds up on the electrode
Zn atoms are oxidized and leave the electrode as Zn²⁺ ions
Zn²⁺ ions are reduced, so the electrode becomes smaller
Cu²⁺ ions that arrive through the salt bridge plate copper onto it
optionWhy: The arrows show electrons being pushed into the Zn electrode, so reduction occurs there: Zn²⁺(aq) + 2 e⁻ → Zn(s). The power supply drives the unfavored reverse of the galvanic reaction, and the Zn electrode gains mass.

A student who thinks the favored reaction occurs whatever power supply is connected picks this. The power supply pushes electrons into the Zn electrode, so the half-reaction there is the reverse of the favored one: Zn²⁺ is reduced.
A student who links reduction with a decrease in size picks this. Reduction of Zn²⁺ deposits zinc metal on the electrode, so it grows and its mass increases.

A student who thinks Cu²⁺ ions travel through the salt bridge to the other electrode picks this. The salt bridge carries K⁺ and NO₃⁻; the ions reduced at the Zn electrode are the Zn²⁺ ions in its own solution.
questions.explain: The arrows show electrons being pushed into the Zn electrode, so reduction occurs there: Zn²⁺(aq) + 2 e⁻ → Zn(s). The power supply drives the unfavored reverse of the galvanic reaction, and the Zn electrode gains mass.

questions.q: A student will build a galvanic cell at 25°C from two of the standard half-cells whose reduction potentials are listed in the table. Which two half-cells give the cell with the largest standard cell potential?
options: Cu and Al half-cells
Ag and Cu half-cells
Al and Mg half-cells
Ag and Mg half-cells
optionWhy: A student who multiplies each E° by its coefficient in the balanced equation picks this: 3(0.34) + 2(1.66) = 4.34 V looks largest. Without multiplying, this cell gives 0.34 − (−1.66) = +2.00 V, less than Ag/Mg.
A student who adds the tabulated reduction potentials picks the two most positive values: 0.80 + 0.34 = 1.14 V. The anode's potential is subtracted, so this cell gives only 0.80 − 0.34 = +0.46 V.
A student who thinks more negative potentials release more energy picks the two most negative values. This pair gives only −1.66 − (−2.37) = +0.71 V.

E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode is largest when the half-reaction with the most positive E° (Ag⁺/Ag, +0.80 V) is paired with the one with the most negative E° (Mg²⁺/Mg, −2.37 V): E°cell = 0.80 − (−2.37) = +3.17 V. No other pair exceeds this (for example, Cu/Mg gives +2.71 V and Ag/Al gives +2.46 V).
questions.explain: E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode is largest when the half-reaction with the most positive E° (Ag⁺/Ag, +0.80 V) is paired with the one with the most negative E° (Mg²⁺/Mg, −2.37 V): E°cell = 0.80 − (−2.37) = +3.17 V. No other pair exceeds this (for example, Cu/Mg gives +2.71 V and Ag/Al gives +2.46 V).

questions.q: The diagram shows a galvanic cell at 25°C made from a standard Ag⁺/Ag half-cell (E° = +0.80 V for Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag) and a standard half-cell of an unknown metal, M, in M(NO₃)₂(aq). The arrows show the direction of electron flow, and the voltmeter shows the cell potential. What is E° for M²⁺(aq) + 2 e⁻ → M(s)?
optionWhy: Electrons flow out of M, so M is the anode and Ag⁺ is reduced at the cathode. 1.05 V = 0.80 V − E°(M²⁺/M), giving E°(M²⁺/M) = −0.25 V.
A student who thinks electrons flow toward the anode, and so takes M²⁺ as the species reduced, picks this: 1.05 = E°(M) − 0.80 gives +1.85 V. Electrons leave the anode, so M is oxidized.

A student who takes the voltmeter reading as the unknown half-cell's potential, made negative because M is oxidized, picks this. The reading is the difference between the two half-cell potentials, and the Ag⁺/Ag half-cell is at +0.80 V, not 0 V.
A student who doubles the Ag⁺/Ag potential because two Ag⁺ ions are reduced per M atom picks this: 1.05 = 2(0.80) − E°(M) gives +0.55 V. E° is not multiplied by coefficients.
questions.explain: Electrons flow out of M, so M is the anode and Ag⁺ is reduced at the cathode. 1.05 V = 0.80 V − E°(M²⁺/M), giving E°(M²⁺/M) = −0.25 V.
questions.working: Electrons leave the M electrode, so M is oxidized (anode) and Ag⁺ is reduced (cathode). E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode: 1.05 V = 0.80 V − E°(M²⁺/M), so E°(M²⁺/M) = 0.80 V − 1.05 V = −0.25 V.

questions.q: A student measures the potentials of four cells at 25°C, each based on Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s), with the concentrations shown in the table. Which claim is supported by the data?
options: E increases as the total concentration of ions in the two solutions increases
E depends on [Cu²⁺], the reactant ion's concentration, and not on [Zn²⁺]
E is greatest when both solutions are at the standard concentration of 1.0 M
E depends on the ratio of [Zn²⁺] to [Cu²⁺], and not on either concentration alone
optionWhy: A student who thinks more ions give a higher potential picks this. Cells 1 and 4 have very different total ion concentrations but the same potential, and cell 3 has fewer ions than cell 1 but a higher potential.
A student who thinks only the reactant ion's concentration matters picks this. Cells 1 and 3 have the same [Cu²⁺] but different potentials, so [Zn²⁺] affects E.
A student who thinks standard conditions give the largest potential picks this. Cell 3, with [Zn²⁺] = 0.10 M, has a higher potential (1.13 V) than cell 1 (1.10 V).

Cells 1 and 4 have the same ratio, [Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺] = 1, and the same potential, although cell 4 is ten times more dilute. A larger ratio (cell 2, ratio 10) gives a lower potential and a smaller ratio (cell 3, ratio 0.1) a higher one, as expected as Q changes.

questions.q: The graph shows how the potential, E, of a galvanic cell at 25°C depends on log Q for the cell reaction. Which statement is supported by the graph?
options: The cell reaction is at equilibrium when Q = 1
Both forward and reverse reactions stop when E falls to 0 V
The cell reaction is at equilibrium when Q = 1 × 10¹⁰
The cell potential would be below E° if Q were less than 1
optionWhy: A student who thinks standard conditions are equilibrium conditions picks this. At Q = 1 (log Q = 0) the graph shows E = E° ≈ 0.30 V, not zero, so the reaction is not at equilibrium.

A student who thinks reactions stop at equilibrium picks this. Where the line reaches E = 0 the cell is at equilibrium: the forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates, so there is no net current.
The potential falls to zero at log Q = 10. E = 0 means there is no driving force: the reaction is at equilibrium, so K = 1 × 10¹⁰.
A student who thinks any departure from standard conditions lowers the potential picks this. The line rises toward smaller log Q, so for Q < 1 (log Q < 0) E would be greater than E°.
questions.explain: The potential falls to zero at log Q = 10. E = 0 means there is no driving force: the reaction is at equilibrium, so K = 1 × 10¹⁰.
questions.working: E = 0 where the line crosses the horizontal axis, at log Q = 10. The cell has no driving force there, so the reaction is at equilibrium: Q = K = 1 × 10¹⁰. At log Q = 0 (Q = 1), E = E° ≈ 0.30 V; for log Q < 0 the line would lie above 0.30 V.
